title: CFA Level I - Session 1 Mock Exam (Paper 3)
description: Full-length 90-question, professional-grade mock exam featuring complex vignettes, realistic calculations, and deep-dive scenarios replicating the true CFA exam difficulty.

questions.text: Consider a portfolio composed of two risky assets, Asset A and Asset B. Asset A has an expected return of 15% and a standard deviation of 21%. Asset B has an expected return of 9% and a standard deviation of 14%. The correlation coefficient between the returns of the two assets is 0.07. If an investor allocates 50% of her funds to Asset A and 50% to Asset B, the expected standard deviation of the portfolio is closest to:
questions.hint: Use the formula: sqrt(wA^2 * stdA^2 + wB^2 * stdB^2 + 2*wA*wB*stdA*stdB*corr)
questions.explanation: Calculation is performed using the portfolio variance formula. The portfolio standard deviation is 13.02%.

questions.text: Elena Rostova, CFA, is a portfolio manager at Meridian Wealth. She recently received a non-public research report from her firm's equity analyst regarding a potential acquisition of NovaTech. The report concludes that NovaTech is severely undervalued. Before the report is distributed to clients, Elena Rostova purchases 1000 shares of NovaTech for her personal account and 18000 shares for her largest institutional client. According to the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, Elena Rostova has most likely violated the standard relating to:
options: Priority of Transactions and Material Nonpublic Information.
questions.hint: Consider the rules around trading on information before clients and trading on non-public info.
questions.explanation: By trading for her personal account before clients, she violates Priority of Transactions. By acting on a non-public internal report regarding an acquisition, she may also be acting on material nonpublic information depending on the source.

questions.text: An economist observes that in the country of Zephyria, the central bank has recently engaged in open market purchases of government securities, decreased the reserve requirement from 9% to 6%, and lowered the policy rate by 75 basis points. Concurrently, the government has increased infrastructure spending and decreased corporate tax rates. The combined effect of these monetary and fiscal policies on Zephyria's aggregate demand (AD) is most likely to be:
options: Indeterminate without knowing the relative magnitudes.
questions.hint: Analyze whether each policy increases or decreases the money supply and government injections.
questions.explanation: Open market purchases, lower reserve requirements, lower policy rates, increased spending, and lower taxes all act to expand the economy and increase aggregate demand.

questions.text: An analyst is evaluating a project with an initial outlay of $500,000. The project is expected to generate cash flows of $173,000 in Year 1, $210,000 in Year 2, $290,000 in Year 3, and $283,000 in Year 4. The company's weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is 10.0%. The net present value (NPV) of the project is closest to:
questions.hint: Discount each cash flow back to present value using the WACC.
questions.explanation: NPV = -Outlay + CF1/(1+r) + CF2/(1+r)^2 + CF3/(1+r)^3 + CF4/(1+r)^4. The exact NPV is $242,001.

questions.text: A manufacturing firm operating under US GAAP reports the following financial data for the year ended December 31: Beginning Inventory of $45000, Purchases of $103000, and Ending Inventory of $48000. During the year, the firm recorded an inventory write-down of $8000 due to obsolescence. If the firm had used IFRS instead of US GAAP, and the net realizable value of the inventory subsequently recovered by $9000 in the following year, the most appropriate accounting treatment under IFRS would be to:
options: Reverse the write-down up to the original cost of the inventory, decreasing COGS.
Recognize the recovery as a direct increase to retained earnings.
Ignore the recovery because inventory reversals are prohibited under IFRS.
questions.hint: IFRS allows reversals of inventory write-downs, unlike US GAAP.
questions.explanation: Under IFRS, if the net realizable value of previously written-down inventory recovers, the write-down can be reversed. The reversal is recognized as a reduction in cost of goods sold (COGS) in the period it occurs, capped at the original cost.

According to the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, Robert Chen has most likely violated the standard relating to:
options: Priority of Transactions and Material Nonpublic Information.
questions.hint: Consider the rules around trading on information before clients and trading on non-public info.
questions.explanation: By trading for her personal account before clients, she violates Priority of Transactions. By acting on a non-public internal report regarding an acquisition, she may also be acting on material nonpublic information depending on the source.

questions.text: Sarah Jenkins, a research analyst at Summit Partners, is preparing a report on the telecommunications sector. He incorporates several paragraphs from a recent industry journal article published by Dr. H. Markowitz into his report. Sarah Jenkins changes a few words in the copied text but does not cite the original author or the journal. According to the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, Sarah Jenkins has violated the Standard relating to:
options: Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients.
questions.hint: Using someone else's work without credit is a specific violation.
questions.explanation: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation strictly prohibits plagiarism. Changing a few words without citing the original source still constitutes plagiarism.

questions.text: An analyst is evaluating a project with an initial outlay of $528,000. The project is expected to generate cash flows of $149,000 in Year 1, $187,000 in Year 2, $296,000 in Year 3, and $281,000 in Year 4. The company's weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is 7.2%. The net present value (NPV) of the project is closest to:
questions.hint: Discount each cash flow back to present value using the WACC.
questions.explanation: NPV = -Outlay + CF1/(1+r) + CF2/(1+r)^2 + CF3/(1+r)^3 + CF4/(1+r)^4. The exact NPV is $226,769.

questions.text: An economist observes that in the country of Gondwana, the central bank has recently engaged in open market purchases of government securities, decreased the reserve requirement from 10% to 5%, and lowered the policy rate by 25 basis points. Concurrently, the government has increased infrastructure spending and decreased corporate tax rates. The combined effect of these monetary and fiscal policies on Gondwana's aggregate demand (AD) is most likely to be:
options: Indeterminate without knowing the relative magnitudes.
questions.hint: Analyze whether each policy increases or decreases the money supply and government injections.
questions.explanation: Open market purchases, lower reserve requirements, lower policy rates, increased spending, and lower taxes all act to expand the economy and increase aggregate demand.

questions.text: A manufacturing firm operating under US GAAP reports the following financial data for the year ended December 31: Beginning Inventory of $50000, Purchases of $141000, and Ending Inventory of $49000. During the year, the firm recorded an inventory write-down of $11000 due to obsolescence. If the firm had used IFRS instead of US GAAP, and the net realizable value of the inventory subsequently recovered by $5000 in the following year, the most appropriate accounting treatment under IFRS would be to:
options: Reverse the write-down up to the original cost of the inventory, decreasing COGS.
Recognize the recovery as a direct increase to retained earnings.
Ignore the recovery because inventory reversals are prohibited under IFRS.
questions.hint: IFRS allows reversals of inventory write-downs, unlike US GAAP.
questions.explanation: Under IFRS, if the net realizable value of previously written-down inventory recovers, the write-down can be reversed. The reversal is recognized as a reduction in cost of goods sold (COGS) in the period it occurs, capped at the original cost.
